title: KV lazy grooming with microbatch-aligned relocation to minimize GPU fragmentation
creator: Priya Kapoor
description:
Problem: Our per-GPU KV cache exhibits slow-growing internal fragmentation under production-style traffic mixes (mixed short and long-context requests, variable token churn). Fragmentation increases peak memory usage and forces evictions that shuffle large KV spans, which in turn increases p99 latency during peak windows. Existing approaches (eager slab coalescing, full-background defrag passes) either introduce unacceptable latency spikes or consume too much copy bandwidth during sustained load.

Goal: Introduce a low-latency, low-bandwidth KV grooming strategy that minimizes fragmentation growth without impacting continuous batching SLOs. The approach must: (1) avoid blocking hot request paths, (2) align relocation work with microbatch boundaries to exploit natural lull points, and (3) localize movement to boundary slots to keep copy volume proportional to fragmentation surface area.

Design summary: "lazy grooming" is a set of coordinated techniques that combine light-weight segmentation metadata, microbatch-aware scheduling, and prioritized relocation lanes. Key ideas: 
- Segment epoch coloring: each KV segment gets a 2-bit color updated on write epochs to detect long-lived holes without scanning contents.
- Slot coloring + heat decay: slots track a lightweight heat counter (byte-sized) that decays over time; cold-to-hot transitions mark candidates for compaction avoidance.
- Microbatch-aligned relocation: the continuous batching layer exposes microbatch boundary hints. We schedule relocation work at these boundaries (microbatch flush points) so grooming happens between request dispatches rather than during active token gen loops.
- Boundary-only coalescing: rather than ripping apart whole slabs, we only move runs at segment boundaries and coalesce adjacent free runs using a small ring of relocation buffers. This keeps copy volume low and targets the actual fragmentation surface.
- Background relocation lanes: two priority lanes—urgent (eviction-driven) and opportunistic (grooming-driven). Urgent runs at high priority and can preempt opportunistic work. Opportunistic only runs when GPU scheduler and continuous-batcher indicate low SLO pressure.
- Occupancy bloom per segment: a small bloom filter indicates if any keys exist in a segment to fast-skip empty segments during scans. Bloom updates are cheap and small (64-bit) and enable O(1) skip decisions on large memory ranges.
- CUDA-friendly copy path: relocation uses CUDA async memcpy with a dedicated stream and page-locked staging buffers when cross-GPU transfers are needed. We respect QoS by limiting relocation bandwidth and using backpressure signals from the I/O stack.

Implementation plan: 
1) Metadata shim: add 1byte/slot heat + 2bit color per segment in header; ensure layout fits in existing descriptor area.
2) Continuous batch hook: extend batcher API to surface microbatch boundary events in a low-overhead callback.
3) Relocation engine: implement boundary-only coalescer that picks runs based on color/heat heuristics and an LRU of fragmentation fences.
4) Bloom filter: integrate a tiny occupancy bloom per 4MB segment; update on key insert/remove in the fast path.
5) Scheduler: implement dual-lane scheduler with dynamic bandwidth cap; expose runtime flags for safe thresholds.
6) Telemetry and safety: add metrics, safety kill-switch, and a conservative default config guarded by a runtime flag.

Trade-offs and notes: 
- Metadata overhead increases memory footprint marginally (~0.5–1%); acceptable given reduction in fragmentation.
- Bloom filters introduce false positives (extra checks) but avoid expensive scans. We tuned filters to have <1% FP with 64-bit counters per segment.
- Microbatch alignment requires cooperation from continuous batching layer; we added a non-blocking hint API to keep integrations simple.
- We accept small relocation bandwidth consumption (configurable) to gain sustained memory compaction; default cap set to 1% of device PCIe bandwidth.

Testing approach: synthetic traces (high-churn short requests, mixed long-context), replay real production traces from the last 30 days, and stress tests that force eviction storms. Measure fragmentation ratio, p99 token latency, compaction bandwidth, and eviction churn.

Rollout strategy: start in internal canary on non-customer-dedicated clusters, then gradual rollout: 1% of traffic -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with rollback on SLO regressions.
acceptance_criteria: Fragmentation ratio (free-run count / total runs) reduced by >=50% vs baseline after 24h of mixed-traffic replay
p99 token generation increase during grooming < 3ms under Production-1 load
Average additional memcpy bandwidth from grooming < 2% of device bandwidth at default cap
False-positive skip rate from bloom filters < 1%
Feature guarded by runtime flag and kill-switch; can be disabled without restarting serving processes
rollout_plan: Spike/POC: run synthetic replay with current allocator vs lazy-grooming to validate heuristics
Internal canary: roll to 2 non-customer clusters, monitor metrics for 48h
Production canary: enable for 1% of traffic (non-critical tenants) with kill-switch
Full rollout: default enabled for runtime-1.20 with opt-out flag for Dedicated customers
comments: 2026-01-13: Spike shows boundary-only coalescing reduces copy volume by ~4x on synthetic churn trace (spike PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/7834)
2026-01-18: Design review with storage team — accepted segment-coloring but asked to reduce color updates to avoid write amplification. We changed color updates to only occur on epoch rollover.
2026-01-21: Benchmarks on A100 cluster: fragmentation ratio down 58% after 12h replay; p99 delta within target at default bandwidth cap.
2026-01-24: Security review not required but infra asked for conservative defaults behind feature flag; added kill-switch and telemetry gating.
2026-01-26: PR opened for relocation engine and bloom integration (https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/7890). Ready for canary when CI passes.
